paras: The Arnaudville night raid on Narcisse Semain's cabin took place in September 1882, when an armed party of white men went at night to the home of Semain, a Black man living near Arnaudville, Louisiana, after a quarrel in the town. Semain shot and killed Marcellus Guitrot, a member of the party, and escaped. Local papers then disputed whether the men had come to punish him or as a constable's posse, and four of them were arrested on Semain's own affidavit.

According to an Opelousas dispatch, a Black man entered a store at Arnaudville, abused the people there and was driven out by the proprietor, Durio, saying he would bring his brothers back. The St. Landry Democrat reported that he returned with his brother, firing a pistol and threatening to shoot the first man he met. In its later account, the Democrat named him as Narcisse Semain of St. Martin's parish, about eight miles below Arnaudville, and said he had insulted A. Durio for refusing credit to another Black man.

The killing was dated to Friday night, September 22, by the first reports and a French-language item in the Thibodaux Sentinel. Guitrot and others went to the cabin, and while they searched for Semain, Guitrot was shot dead by someone hidden in an adjoining cotton patch. The Democrat's first item instead said the man lay hidden along the road and fired into the approaching party. Semain escaped, and the party left with Guitrot's body.

The St. Martins Observer reported that Semain swore an affidavit charging the men with coming to kill him and trying to set fire to his house. Adelin Durio, Adam Guidroz, Lucien Roy and Maura Bernard, described as a colored man, were arrested and bailed by Judge T. Fontelieu to appear before the District Court, with no preliminary examination. No report of a trial of these men or of any charge against Semain was found in the coverage.

The Lafayette Advertiser wrote that Guitrot and his friends meant to "make short work" of the man and were forcing entry when he fired. The St. Landry Democrat, citing "responsible parties," called this "very erroneous" and said town constable Angelas Durio had summoned a posse to arrest Semain on an affidavit for violating town ordinances. By that account the door was open with only an infant inside, Semain was promised safety if he surrendered, and Guitrot was shot as he approached the cotton patch. The Advertiser answered that it was "extraordinary" for the slayer of a posse member to have that posse arrested, and for its members to waive an examination.

The Opelousas dispatch, printed in the Lake Charles Commercial, headlined the killing "An Assassination" and called Semain a "negro desperado," while the Democrat's first item called him a "colored desparado." The Advertiser took the opposite line, remarking that the Black man "ought to have prepared a rope for this well meaning party." The Thibodaux Sentinel and the Donaldsonville Chief carried short state-news items, the latter saying the white men came to punish him for "offensive conduct." Coverage ran from September 30 to October 21, 1882, and was confined to Louisiana weeklies; the reports spelled the names variously as Guitrot or Guidroz and Semain, Semere or Semene.

reader.title: Arnaudville night raid on Narcisse Semain's cabin
bases: An armed party of white men went at night to a Black man's cabin, to punish him by most accounts (A4, A5 quoting the Advertiser, A6) or to arrest him as a constable's posse by the Democrat's account (A5); he shot and killed one of them and escaped (A1, A2).

Several independent reports agree a night party went to the Black man's cabin and one of its members, Guitrot or Guidroz, was killed (A1, A2, A3, A4, A6), but the Democrat denies the Advertiser's account of a punishing party and forcible entry, calling it a lawful posse (A5, A6).

accounts.label: St. Landry Democrat's 'responsible parties'
accounts.gist: A constable's posse came to arrest Semain under an ordinance affidavit, found the door open with only an infant inside, called on him to surrender, and Guitrot was shot approaching the cotton patch.

framing.detail: The Opelousas dispatch headlined it 'An Assassination' and called the shooter a 'negro desperado'; the Democrat's first item called him a 'colored desparado'.
The Lafayette Advertiser ironically called the party 'well meaning' and later questioned the posse story given the arrests on the Black man's affidavit.
The St. Landry Democrat called the Advertiser's account 'very erroneous' and presented the party as a lawful posse.
The Thibodaux Sentinel and Donaldsonville Chief ran one-line state-news items.
